prompt: An engineer proposes defeating a fixed AWGN channel's Shannon limit simply by using more modulation states, without changing bandwidth or received signal-to-noise power ratio. What is the problem?

options.text: Decibels are the power ratio itself, so no conversion is ever needed
options.explanation: A decibel value is logarithmic; it is not the linear power ratio.

options.text: More states cannot remove the noisy-channel capacity limit; they must still be reliably distinguished
options.explanation: Correct. Suitable signalling and coding can approach the modelled limit, but cannot exceed it under unchanged channel assumptions.

options.text: Shannon capacity promises every finite packet is error-free below the limit
options.explanation: The coding result is asymptotic; finite implementations still have error probabilities and constraints.

options.text: Capacity is set only by the chosen modulation name
options.explanation: Channel bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio set the stated capacity; modulation is part of an implementation.

workedExample: The receiver observes noisy signals. Adding more choices can pack them closer together without creating more reliable distinctions. Capacity constrains the reliable information rate for the stated channel, while signalling and coding determine how effectively an implementation uses it. An SNR quoted in decibels must also be interpreted as a logarithmic power ratio.

prompt: For a single flat AWGN channel at high SNR, compare doubling bandwidth while holding SNR fixed with doubling signal power while holding bandwidth and noise fixed. Which raises the capacity limit more?

options.text: Doubling signal power must double capacity
options.explanation: At high SNR, capacity grows only logarithmically with the power ratio.

options.text: Doubling bandwidth: it doubles capacity under the stated fixed-SNR assumption
options.explanation: Correct. The proportional bandwidth effect is larger than the high-SNR gain from doubling signal power.

options.text: Both have the same effect because both are called doubling
options.explanation: They affect different parts of the channel relationship.

options.text: Neither changes capacity because modulation alone fixes the limit
options.explanation: Capacity describes the channel constraint, not a fixed modulation scheme.

workedExample: Hold each comparison's assumptions carefully. Fixed-SNR bandwidth expansion scales the channel capacity directly. At high SNR, doubling signal power gives a smaller proportional gain because of diminishing returns. If total signal power instead stayed fixed while bandwidth and admitted noise grew, the SNR would fall; that is a different comparison. Actual Wi-Fi adds contention, coding, pilots and protocol overhead.
